text: I
'm working through the DIY versus professional training decision for this adol
escent border collie mix. The dog has two interconnected issues—barking at every other dog and pulling hard
—that likely stem from frustrated greeting behavior and over-arousal rather than fear-based aggression,
which makes sense given the breed, age, and rescue background. I
need to assess the body language more carefully to confirm this, but the key
question is whether this is something manageable on my own over a few weeks or if it requires
professional intervention.
The
timing of counterconditioning is where things get tricky, and that's where a
certified positive trainer becomes valuable. My best approach is hybrid: start the DIY plan immediately
since the first week or two focuses on management and foundational work that's hard to mess
up, then layer in the $360 Reactive Dog class as the professional component. That class gives
me something I can't replicate at home—controlled, predictable exposure to other dogs at a managed
distance, which is the actual bottleneck in DIY reactivity work. The AKC emphasizes that you need to control the environment and coordinate
with friends who have dogs, but a reactive dog class essentially provides that infrastructure ready-made.
If red flags emerge during this process, I'll escalate to a private trainer or veter
inary behaviorist.
I
'm gathering research on loose-leash walking mechanics and engagement techniques to ground the
4-week plan — I've got solid material from AKC guidance on
management and equipment, the LAT game, threshold measurement approaches, and front-clip harness training to
work from.
Now
I'm laying out the 4-week training plan, starting with the equipment needed before beginning
—a front-clip harness to prevent neck strain, a standard 6-foot leash as required
, a treat pouch, and high-value rewards like meat strips and cheese to keep the dog motivated
throughout the program.
I
'm identifying two main training threads running in parallel: loose-leash mechanics in controlled
, low-distraction settings, and emotional regulation work using an engage/disengage protocol with a
clicker. The third critical piece is management—preventing the dog from rehearsing reactive
behavior while also addressing the underlying arousal from unmet enrich

ment needs, which is especially important for a border collie's herding drive.

Week 1 focuses on establishing a
baseline: acquiring the equipment, fitting the harness properly, and identifying the exact threshold distance where the dog first fixates on
other dogs versus when barking begins, so I know where
to work from.
By
end of week one, he should be able to state his threshold distance, identify whether he's a
frustrated or fearful reactor, keep blow-ups to two or fewer, and execute
the U-turn reliably with no dogs around. Week two shifts to
engagement work at a safe distance—three to four
short sessions where you let him notice passing dogs, then click and reward the moment he looks
away, staying at whatever distance lets him succeed without
reacting. Keep loose-leash walking to
quiet streets during this phase and don't push closer yet
Week
three introduces the disengagement cue where you wait for him to naturally
look away from the dog before clicking, then gradually close the distance in small steps once he's n
ailing three to five clean reps. If he fixates for more than five seconds, drop back to the easier version
. You'll also start building an alternative behavior like a hand touch or "
find it" in a calm setting first.
By
the end of week three, the threshold distance should noticeably shrink and he
should handle a level two rep even when the other dog is moving.
Week four is about generalizing this to different dogs since the association needs to be rebuilt across multiple examples,
and you can start parallel walking at a distance with help from a friend or class. The goal
isn't necessarily a dog-park dog—passing calmly at a distance by crossing the street or putting
a car between you is a perfectly valid outcome.
The
end-of-week marker is hitting three different dogs below threshold, passing a calm dog on the far side of a residential street without escal
ating, and managing five minutes of loose-leash walking on a normal street. The biggest mistakes that derail progress are punishing the barking instead
of changing how the dog feels, working too close when he won't take food, using treats that aren't high-value enough
against the distraction, relying only on random encounters
instead of controlled setups, running sessions too long, and
advancing
distance in yards rather than incremental steps. Management is critical—letting
him rehearse the reaction repeatedly undoes the training. The goal is calm
passing, not greeting, and loose-leash walking should happen separately from reactivity work in
dog-free areas. A retractable leash or neck collar won

't work for a hard puller.

## What I concluded

**1. Hire or DIY — do
both, cheaply.** Start the self-directed plan this week and book *one* $360 class. Don't start with a $2,400 private program. The reas
oning: the hard part of fixing leash reactivity yourself isn't the technique, it's that the
method needs another dog to appear at a distance *you* choose and then leave — which normal walks never prov

ide. A reactive-dog class is precisely that setup with someone watching your timing.

**2. Three options,

real prices.** The winner is clear:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **South Bay Dog Training**, Campbell | Reactive Dog 1 — 4 in-person + 5 Zoom Q&As +

daily support | **$360** |
| D For Dogz, San Jose→Palo Alto | Private coaching, 6 wks | $2,400 |

| HSSV, Milpitas | Manners, 6 sessions | $200 |

Campbell bans prong/choke/e-collars, is CCP
DT + Fear Free credentialed, and runs weekends *and* evenings. **Time-sensitive catch:** the Aug 16 Sunday 11am section

is full, but their page says a 12pm section can be added if there's interest — so that email matters now.

I ruled out
Off Leash K9 San Jose on method: every package includes an e-collar, and teaching a dog that another dog's appearance predicts pain is the wrong lesson for a problem about

how he *feels*.

**3. Four weeks**, built on the Engage/Disengage protocol. Week 1 has de
liberately *no* trigger training — you measure his threshold in feet and re-route walks so he stops rehearsing the barking. Weeks 2–4 run

Level 1, then Level 2 with distance closing in *steps*, then generalising across different dogs.

## One judgement call

worth your attention

I've argued he's most likely a **frustrated greeter** — a 14-month herding mix barking at *every* dog usually wants to get to
them, not away. That's the more optimistic read and those dogs improve faster. But it's an inference from your description, not an observation, so Week 1

's subtask tells you how to confirm it from body language. Bring the answer to the first class; it changes what the trainer does with him.

so you may well qualify) → buy the kit → start Week 1. First two are 15 minutes each.
